The Lighthouse at Gull Point

Chapter 1: The Storm Bell

The wind came off the sea like a living thing, and the old lighthouse groaned on its foundations. Mara Quill climbed the iron stairs two at a time, her lantern swinging wild shadows across the stone.

"Tobias!" she shouted up the stairwell. "The bell! Ring the bell!"

From the lamp room came a muffled reply. "I can't reach the rope, it's jammed!" Tobias was only twelve, and his voice cracked with fright.

Thunder split the sky. Somewhere below, a shutter tore loose and slammed against the wall, again and again, like a fist on a door.

Mara reached the top and pushed past the boy. The bell rope had wound itself around the gear housing. She drew her knife and sawed at the tangle.

"Stand back," she said, quieter now. "When this comes free it'll swing."

The rope parted with a snap. The great bronze bell swung out over the sea and rang, once, twice, a deep note that rolled across the water toward the dark shape of the ship on the reef.

"Do you think they heard?" Tobias asked.

"They heard," said Mara. She did not know if it was true.


Chapter 2: The Stranger

Morning came grey and quiet. The storm had blown itself out, and the sea lay flat and sullen under a low sky. Gulls cried over the rocks.

They found the man on the shingle below the point, half in the water, wrapped in a torn oilskin. He was alive.

"Easy," Mara said, kneeling beside him. "You're on Gull Point. You're safe."

The stranger opened his eyes. They were a startling pale green. "The Corvid," he whispered. "My ship. Did anyone else..."

"Only you, so far," she said. "What's your name?"

"Ansel. Ansel Vey." He coughed, and seawater ran from the corner of his mouth. "First mate. There were nine of us."

Tobias came running down the path with blankets, his boots crunching on the stones. "Is he a pirate?" the boy asked, breathless.

Ansel laughed, a dry rattle that turned into another cough. "Not today, lad."

Later, in the keeper's cottage, a fire crackled in the grate and a kettle began to whistle. Mara poured tea and set the cup in Ansel's shaking hands.

"You rang the bell," he said. It was not a question.

"We did."

"Then you saved my life. The others were already in the boats when the mast came down." He stared into the fire. "I'll not forget it."

Old Hetta, who kept the cottage and had seen sixty winters on the point, sniffed from her chair by the door. "Fine words," she said. "Words don't mend a roof. That shutter's clean gone."

"Hetta," Mara warned.

"I'm only saying." The old woman went back to her knitting, needles clicking.


Chapter 3: The Letter

A week passed. Ansel mended the shutter, and then the gate, and then the leaking window in the lamp room, whistling as he worked. Tobias followed him everywhere.

On the seventh day a rider came up the cliff road, hooves ringing on the stone. He carried a letter sealed with black wax.

Mara read it standing in the doorway. Her face did not change, but her hand tightened on the paper until it crumpled.

"What is it?" Ansel asked.

"The Harbour Board," she said. "They're closing the light. Come spring, there'll be a new one on the north shore, all electric. We're to leave by the first of March."

Tobias looked from one to the other. "Leave? But where would we go?"

Nobody answered him. Outside, the sea went on breaking against the rocks, as it always had, and the wind rose softly in the eaves.

Hetta set down her knitting. "Well," she said. "I suppose someone had better put the kettle on."
